Jump-Start a Car Safely

Safety first: Never let the red and black clamps touch. Wear eye protection if you have it.

user_name, dead battery? Here's the order that keeps sparks away.

  1. Park the good car close, engines off. Set both parking brakes.
  2. Connect red clamp to positive (+) of dead battery.
  3. Connect other red clamp to positive (+) of good battery.
  4. Connect black clamp to negative (-) of good battery.
  5. Connect other black clamp to a bare metal bolt on the dead car's engine block (not the battery).
  6. Start the good car, let it run a few minutes, then start the dead car.
  7. Once running, remove clamps in reverse order.
Why not connect black to dead battery?
The last connection can spark. Connecting to the engine block moves the spark away from battery gases.

Fixing a Stripped Screw

Don't dig. user_name, digging widens the hole and makes it worse.

  1. Rubber band. Lay a wide rubber band over the head, press hard, turn slowly. Grips the stripped edges.
  2. Bigger bit. Step up one size so the driver bites fresh metal.
  3. Left-hand drill bit. Spins counter-clockwise, so it often backs the screw out on its own.
  4. Screw extractor. Drill a small pilot hole, then twist the extractor in with a wrench.
  5. Last resort. Cut a slot with a rotary tool and use a flathead.
Safety glasses. Tiny metal shavings have terrible aim.
Why screws strip in the first place

Usually three things: the wrong bit size, too little downward pressure, or a bitator bit that's rounded off at the tip. Replace worn bits early.

Cleaning a Cast-Iron Skillet

Short version, user_name: wash, dry fast, oil thin, done.

  1. Wash while warm. Hot water, stiff brush. A little mild soap is fine on modern seasoning.
  2. Scrub stuck bits with coarse salt and a splash of oil — no steel wool.
  3. Dry on the stove. Low heat for a couple minutes until every drop is gone. Rust starts in moisture.
  4. Oil thin. A few drops of neutral oil, wiped with a paper towel until it looks almost dry.
  5. Store dry. A folded paper towel between stacked pans keeps air moving.
Don't soak it. Don't air-dry it. Cast iron holds grudges.
What if it's already rusty?

Scrub the rust off with steel wool or fine sandpaper, wash, dry, then re-season: thin oil, 45 minutes in a 450°F oven, upside down.

Cleaning a Dishwasher Filter

A clogged filter makes dishes gritty and the dishwasher smelly. Most manufacturers recommend cleaning it monthly. It's a five-minute job.

  1. Remove the bottom rack. The filter is usually a cylindrical mesh screen at the base.
  2. Twist the filter counterclockwise and lift it out. Some models have two parts: a coarse and a fine filter.
  3. Rinse under warm running water. Use a soft brush (an old toothbrush works) to scrub away grease and food bits.
  4. For stubborn buildup, soak in warm soapy water for 10 minutes, then rinse.
  5. Reinstall and run a hot cycle with a cup of white vinegar in the top rack to freshen the whole machine.
Clean filter = cleaner dishes and no more funky smell. Add it to your monthly routine.

Tame the cable octopus

A few loops and a twist tie beat any fancy gadget.

  1. Loop the cable loosely around your hand—about four fingers wide.
  2. Slide the loop off and wrap a twist tie or Velcro strap around the middle.
  3. Don’t coil it tight around the plug; that’s where breaks start.

Bonus: label each one with a bit of masking tape.

Crunch time

The secret is dry, dry, dry—and a hot oven.

400°F / 200°C25–35 min
  1. Drain and rinse a can of chickpeas. Pat them very dry with a towel.
  2. Pick off any loose skins—they burn before the insides crisp.
  3. Toss with a tablespoon of oil and salt. Spread on a sheet pan in one layer.
  4. Roast, shaking the pan every 10 minutes, until they rattle and taste crunchy.

They soften as they cool, so eat them soon.

instances.title: Tightening a Wobbly Chair Leg
instances.html:
No more rocking

Most wobbles are just a loose screw or a tired hole.

If the screw is loose

Turn the chair over. Tighten the screw or bolt with a screwdriver. Don’t overtighten—wood can crack.

If the screw spins in place

Dip a toothpick in wood glue, push it into the hole, snap it off flush. Then reinsert the screw. The wood fibers give it something to bite.

For metal chairs, a drop of thread-locking fluid works.

The white stuff

Gray happens when soil redeposits. Separate and boost.

Wash whites separatelyWarm water
  • Wash whites only with other whites—no light grays or creams.
  • Use a detergent with enzymes and a scoop of oxygen bleach (not chlorine).
  • Add a half-cup of white vinegar to the rinse to strip residue.

Skip fabric softener—it leaves a waxy film that traps dirt.

instances.title: Fixing a Zipper That Splits Open
instances.html:
Zip it back

Usually the slider has spread. A squeeze can save it.

  1. Move the slider to the bottom of the zipper.
  2. With pliers, gently squeeze the top and bottom of the slider—just a hair.
  3. Test the zipper. Repeat if it still splits.

Go slow. One too-hard squeeze and the slider won’t move at all.
